28539:
Hezekiah son of Ahaz was king of Judah at the turning point of the Assyrian age. Inheriting a kingdom that his father had made an Assyrian vassal and whose temple had been closed, he reopened and purified the temple, held a Passover to which he invited the survivors of the fallen northern kingdom, and removed local shrines and even Moses' bronze serpent. Kings says there was none like him among the kings of Judah in trusting the LORD.

His reign is also one of the best-attested in the ancient Near East. He prepared Jerusalem for war, cutting the water tunnel that still runs under the City of David, and in 701 BC faced Sennacherib's invasion. Assyrian annals boast of shutting him up in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage' and receiving heavy tribute; the biblical account agrees on the tribute but climaxes in the city's deliverance after Hezekiah's prayer and Isaiah's oracle.

The narrative does not idealise him. After his recovery from a mortal illness, he proudly showed Babylonian envoys his treasures and received Isaiah's announcement of future exile with relief that it would not come in his own lifetime. He is remembered as a model of reforming, praying kingship who nevertheless left a son, Manasseh, who undid his reforms.
28540: Kings, Chronicles and Isaiah each narrate his reign (2 Kgs 18:1-20:21; 2 Chr 29:1-32:33; Isa 36:1-39:8). The text states he trusted the LORD and held fast to him (2 Kgs 18:5-6), rebelled against Assyria (2 Kgs 18:7), paid tribute to Sennacherib (2 Kgs 18:14-16), prayed for deliverance (2 Kgs 19:15-19), was granted fifteen more years (2 Kgs 20:6), and was rebuked for his display to Babylon (2 Kgs 20:16-18). Chronicles adds his temple restoration and Passover and notes that God left him to test him (2 Chr 32:31). Proverbs credits his men with copying proverbs of Solomon (Prov 25:1).
28541: Rabbinic tradition praises Hezekiah as a king who spread Torah study throughout the land, and the Talmud credits 'Hezekiah and his company' with writing down Isaiah, Proverbs, Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes (b. Bava Batra 15a). Some sages said he could have been the Messiah but failed to sing praise after his deliverance (b. Sanhedrin 94a).
28542: Read as a type of faithful prayer and reform; his song in Isa 38:10-20 is used as a canticle in the Liturgy of the Hours (Lauds), and he appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:9-10).
28543: Frequently held up as the model reformer who restores pure worship according to the word, even destroying a venerable relic (the bronze serpent) when it became an object of misplaced devotion; his response to Isaiah's oracle is read as a caution about short-sighted faith.
28544: Many scholars see the account as shaped by later Deuteronomistic editors who made Hezekiah a forerunner of Josiah. Debate continues over whether 2 Kgs 18:13-16 and 18:17-19:37 preserve one campaign or two, and over the internal chronology (2 Kgs 18:1 versus 18:13).
28545: Restored temple worship immediately on accession
28546: Trusted God and prayed under overwhelming threat
28547: Practical and far-sighted preparations for siege
28549: Rebelled against Assyria in alliance-seeking that Isaiah criticised (Isa 30:1-5)
28551: Displayed his treasures to Babylon and was complacent about the coming exile
28552: Opening the temple in his first month
28556: Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC, early in or just before his reign, leaving Judah alone between Assyria and Egypt. Archaeology supplies unusual corroboration: Sennacherib's annals (Taylor and Oriental Institute prisms), the Lachish reliefs from Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh, the Siloam tunnel inscription, the Broad Wall in Jerusalem, thousands of royal (lmlk) storage-jar handles, and a clay seal impression reading 'Belonging to Hezekiah son of Ahaz, king of Judah' found on the Ophel in 2009 and published in 2015.
28557: Hezekiah became the standard of the trusting reformer-king alongside Josiah (2 Kgs 18:5; 2 Kgs 23:25). Jeremiah's contemporaries remembered that he heeded Micah's warning (Jer 26:18-19), and Ben Sira praises him for fortifying the city and bringing water into it (Sirach 48:17-22).
28558: Hezekiah and his circle are credited with writing down (editing) Isaiah, Proverbs, the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes.
28559: Hezekiah is said to have hidden away a 'book of remedies' so that people would pray rather than rely on it, an act the sages approved.
28561: Earnest and devout, quick to tear his clothes and pray aloud, but also a shrewd planner who talks of tunnels, walls and storehouses; under praise he can slip into self-satisfaction.
28567: Building and fortification after his restoration

28571: Kings says he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood and later names his sins as the reason judgment on Judah could not be averted.

28576: Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, reigned fifty-five years in the seventh century BC as a loyal vassal of Assyria. Kings presents him as the worst king of Judah, reversing his father's reforms, introducing astral and Canaanite cults into the temple, sacrificing his son, and shedding innocent blood, so that his reign becomes the stated reason for the exile. Chronicles adds a striking twist: taken captive to Babylon, he repented, prayed, and was restored, becoming a picture of grace for the worst of sinners.
28577: 2 Kgs 21:1-18 records only his apostasy and violence and later blames the exile on his sins (2 Kgs 23:26; 2 Kgs 24:3-4; Jer 15:4). 2 Chr 33:1-20 records the same sins but adds his captivity, repentance and partial reform.

28581: Some see the Chronicler's repentance account as theological reinterpretation explaining his long reign; others note Assyrian records of vassal kings summoned to court as making a captivity plausible.
28582: He appears as 'Menasi king of Judah' in Assyrian lists of vassals supplying building materials and troops under Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal. His long reign coincides with the height of Assyrian power.
28583: His name became shorthand for the apostasy that sealed Judah's fate, and his reported repentance became a classic example of the reach of divine mercy.
28584: Isaiah was put to death by Manasseh, sawn in two while hiding in a tree.
28585: Ascension of Isaiah 5:1-14; Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 49b
28586: A penitential prayer composed by Manasseh in captivity has been preserved (the Prayer of Manasseh).
28588: Polished, worldly and pragmatic, speaking the language of empire and omens; in the Chronicler's telling, broken and plain-spoken in his repentance.

28621:
Josiah came to the throne of Judah as an eight-year-old after his father Amon was assassinated, and became the most thorough reformer in the history of the monarchy. In his eighteenth year (622 BC), workers repairing the temple found 'the book of the law'. Its reading shook the king; he consulted the prophetess Huldah, gathered the people for a covenant renewal, and launched a purge of foreign cults and local shrines that reached as far as Bethel and the towns of the former northern kingdom, followed by a Passover unmatched since the judges.

Kings gives him its highest praise: no king before or after turned to the LORD with all his heart, soul and might as he did (2 Kgs 23:25). Yet the same narrative states that the reform did not reverse the judgment provoked by Manasseh. In 609 BC Josiah went out to Megiddo against Pharaoh Necho and was killed, aged thirty-nine. Within twenty-three years Jerusalem fell.

Josiah stands at the centre of modern discussion of Deuteronomy and the Deuteronomistic History, since many scholars identify the rediscovered book with some form of Deuteronomy. His reign also forms the background to the early ministries of Jeremiah and Zephaniah.
28622: 2 Kgs 22:1-23:30 and 2 Chr 34:1-35:27 narrate his reign. Kings centres the reform on the finding of the book (2 Kgs 22:8); Chronicles places the start of the purge six years earlier (2 Chr 34:3). The text predicts his name centuries ahead (1 Kgs 13:2), states that he was unmatched in his turning to the LORD (2 Kgs 23:25), and that the LORD's anger against Judah nevertheless remained (2 Kgs 23:26-27). Chronicles says Necho warned him that God had sent Necho and that Josiah did not listen to words from God's mouth (2 Chr 35:21-22). Jeremiah praises his justice for the poor and needy (Jer 22:15-16).
28623: Remembered as a righteous king; the Talmud (b. Taanit 22b) explains his death as a failure to consult Jeremiah before engaging Necho, and tradition holds he hid the ark to protect it from exile (b. Yoma 52b).
28624: Read as an example of revival through rediscovery of the word of God, and of personal faithfulness amid national decline; he appears in Matthew's genealogy (Matt 1:10-11).
28625: Often cited as a model of reformation by Scripture: the book is read, the heart is cut, the covenant is renewed and worship is purified. Some preachers also stress his death as a warning against acting without seeking God's guidance.
28626: Since W. M. L. de Wette (1805) many identify the book with Deuteronomy or an early core of it, and many argue the first edition of Kings was produced to support Josiah's centralisation. Others think the 'finding' account is a later legitimising narrative, and a minority doubt the reform's scope; the debate is ongoing.
28628: Responded to Scripture with repentance and action
28630: Defended the cause of the poor and needy
28631: Engaged Necho in battle against warning and was killed (2 Chr 35:22)
28633: Hearing the book of the law read
28636: Assyria was collapsing in Josiah's reign (Nineveh fell in 612 BC), opening a window for Judah to reassert control over former northern territory. Necho II was marching to aid the Assyrian remnant against Babylon at Harran and Carchemish when Josiah met him; the Babylonian Chronicle helps date these events.
28637: Josiah became the ideal king in Deuteronomistic perspective and a fixed point for dating prophets (Jer 1:2; Zeph 1:1). His death was so grieved that lamentation for him became an annual custom (2 Chr 35:25), and his reforms shaped the Torah-centred faith that survived the exile.

Torn between his officials' pro-Egyptian rebellion and Jeremiah's call to submit to Babylon, he wavered, broke his oath to Nebuchadnezzar, and saw Jerusalem besieged and destroyed. His capture, blinding and exile mark the end of the Davidic monarchy in the land.

28682: Hebrew poetry and rhetoric of the highest order

28694: Walks barefoot and stripped for three years

28708:
Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem for about forty years in the second half of the eighth century BC, through the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. He moved in royal circles, counselled kings face to face, and was married to a woman he calls 'the prophetess'; he gave his sons symbolic names. His call vision in the temple, with its threefold 'Holy', shaped his whole message: the Holy One of Israel demands trust rather than political alliances, judges pride and injustice, and will preserve a remnant.

The book bearing his name is the longest and most quoted prophetic book in the New Testament. Its first part addresses the Assyrian crises of Ahaz and Hezekiah; chapters 36-39 narrate the deliverance of Jerusalem in 701 BC; chapters 40-66 speak to exiles in Babylon and to the restored community, naming Cyrus and presenting the Servant of the LORD. Whether all of this comes from Isaiah himself is one of the classic debates of biblical scholarship.

Isaiah's language of a virgin or young woman bearing Immanuel, a child called Mighty God, a shoot from Jesse's stump, and a Servant 'wounded for our transgressions' became central to Christian proclamation of Jesus, while in Judaism the book is above all the great prophet of consolation read in the synagogue after the ninth of Av.
